abstract.para: Kernel boot parameters tell the kernel how to behave at startup. Knowing where they come from and how &grub; passes them to the kernel makes it easier to change them correctly. This knowledge also helps you reason about which change to make for a given problem.

section.title: What are kernel boot parameters?
section.para: Kernel boot parameters are configurations passed to the kernel during the boot process managed by &grub;. The configurations are instructions to the &grub; boot loader on how to configure certain features and make them behave in the intended manner. The method of modification depends on whether you want the change to affect only the next boot, or all subsequent boots.

section.title: Methods of modification
section.para: You can modify the kernel boot parameters using the following methods:

listitem.para: Changes are held in memory and apply only to the upcoming boot process. These changes made through the &grub; boot menu are not written to any configuration file and are discarded after reboot.

Changes are written to the /etc/default/grub file and persist across all subsequent boot processes. For permanent changes, we recommend using the update-bootloader command instead of directly editing the /etc/default/grub file.

However, if you directly edit the /etc/default/grub file, modify the GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX or GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT variables. After modification, regenerate the &grub; configuration by running the following command with administrative privileges.

section.title: Benefits of modifying kernel boot parameters
section.para: A few common reasons to modify kernel boot parameters:

formalpara.title: Performance
formalpara.para: Tune the kernel for a specific workload. For example, the quiet parameter suppresses most boot messages, which shortens boot time.

formalpara.title: Hardware compatibility
formalpara.para: Work around a hardware quirk the kernel misdetects by default. For example, the acpi=off parameter disables the Advanced Configuration and Power Interface (ACPI), which can resolve boot problems on older hardware.

formalpara.title: Troubleshooting
formalpara.para: Isolate a driver or subsystem that is preventing the system from booting. For instance, the nomodeset parameter disables kernel mode setting, which helps when a graphics driver prevents the system from booting.

section.title: Examples of commonly modified kernel boot parameters
section.para: A few of the most commonly modified kernel boot parameters:

listitem.para: Specifies the path to the root file system.
Suppresses most boot messages.
Displays a graphical boot splash screen.
Disables kernel mode setting.
Enables debugging output.
Toggles the Advanced Configuration and Power Interface (ACPI) settings.

section.para: When modifying kernel boot parameters, follow these essential formatting rules:

listitem.para: Separate individual parameters with a single space:
With update-bootloader, add each parameter with its own --add-option call. The command inserts the spacing for you:
In the /etc/default/grub configuration file for &grub;, use spaces between kernel parameters when passing them as string values to the GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX or GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT variables.
At the boot menu, press E to edit, locate the line starting with linux, and add parameters with spaces.
